title: The Tell-Tale Heart
author: Edgar Allan Poe
sourceEdition: The Pioneer (1843), Project Gutenberg plain-text edition

premise.en: A nameless narrator insists he is not mad, even as he confesses, in obsessive and feverish detail, to murdering an old man over nothing more than the look of his pale, clouded eye.

summary.en: An unnamed narrator, desperate to prove his own sanity, describes how he came to hate a single filmy, vulture-like eye belonging to the old man he lives with, and how, over seven nights, he crept into the old man's room to watch him sleep before finally killing him. He hides the body beneath the floorboards with methodical calm, but when the police arrive on a neighbor's report, an unbearable sound rising from beneath his own feet begins to unravel him.

contentWarning: The narrator confesses in graphic detail to murdering and dismembering the old man he lives with.

tutorNotes.pronunciation: Poe's narrator speaks in long, breathless bursts, so practice reading whole sentences aloud without stopping for breath at every comma, letting the rising intensity carry through dashes and exclamation marks the way the original punctuation intends.
tutorNotes.grammar: This text leans on free indirect narration and long periodic sentences that delay their main verb, building suspense before the sentence resolves; watch also for the past perfect used to describe the narrator's careful preparations before each night's events. Dashes function almost as a second kind of punctuation, marking sudden shifts in the narrator's feverish thought.
tutorNotes.culture: Poe wrote in the 1840s, when houses of this kind commonly had no electric light, so a single dark lantern with a shuttered opening, as the narrator carries, was a realistic tool for moving unseen through a dark room at night. Nineteenth-century American law also allowed police to investigate a household on a neighbor's report of a scream, without any warrant, exactly as happens near the story's end.
tutorNotes.commonErrors: Learners often confuse 'conscience' (an inner sense of right and wrong) with 'consciousness' (the state of being awake and aware), both of which shadow the narrator's account. Note also that 'mad' here means 'insane,' an older usage distinct from the more common modern sense of 'angry.'

question.en: What reason does the narrator give for wanting to kill the old man, and what does this reveal about his state of mind?
How does the narrator behave during the seven nights before the murder, and what does this routine suggest about him?
How does the narrator dispose of the body, and how does he behave when the police arrive?
What does the narrator hear as he speaks with the police, and where does that sound most likely come from?
Why might the narrator's constant insistence that he is not mad actually convince the reader of the opposite?

chapters.title: Chapter 1 — The Eye
paragraphs: True! Nervous, very, very dreadfully nervous I had been and am — but why will you say that I am mad?
The disease had sharpened my senses, not destroyed, not dulled them.
Above all, my sense of hearing had grown unnaturally, almost unbearably acute.
I heard all things in the heaven and in the earth, and I heard many things in hell besides — and I have never once mistaken this for madness.
Listen, then, and observe how healthily, how calmly, I can tell you the whole story of what happened.
You will surely think me mad when I have finished, and yet it is impossible to say how first the idea entered my brain.
Once conceived, it haunted me day and night, and would give me no rest at all.
Object there was none, and passion there was none; I loved the old man dearly.
He had never once wronged me or insulted my pride, and for his gold I had no desire whatsoever.
He kept none of any value hidden about his simple, unremarkable person, nor in his sparsely furnished room.
I believe it was his eye — yes, it was this alone that so troubled and tormented me.
It was a pale blue eye, filmed over like the eye of some patient vulture.
Whenever it fell upon me, my blood ran cold with a horror I could not name or reason away.
So, slowly, very slowly, I made up my mind to take the old man's life, and thereby to rid myself of the eye forever.
Now this is the point: you fancy me mad, but madmen know nothing of true caution.
You should have seen with what wisdom, what foresight, I proceeded with my terrible task.
I was never kinder to the old man than during the whole week before I finally killed him.
Every night, about midnight, I turned the latch of his door and opened it, oh, so gently.
When I had made an opening sufficient for my head, I put in a dark lantern, closed so that no light shone from it at all.
Then I thrust in my head, very, very slowly indeed, until it took me a full hour to see him lying upon his bed.
Would a madman have been so wise as this, so patient and so precise in every small movement?
And when my head was well inside the room, I undid the lantern cautiously, for its hinges creaked, letting a single thin ray of light fall upon that vulture eye.

chapters.title: Chapter 2 — Seven Nights
paragraphs: This I did for seven long nights, always precisely at midnight.
But I always found the old man's eye closed, and so it was impossible to accomplish the terrible work I had set myself.
It was not the old man himself who vexed me, you understand, but rather his cursed, filmy eye.
Each morning I greeted him cheerfully, asking how he had passed the night, without a hint of my true purpose.
He would have had to be a very profound old man indeed to suspect that every single night, precisely at twelve, I looked in upon him while he lay there, deeply and peacefully asleep.
Upon the eighth night, however, I proceeded to open the door with even greater caution than usual.
I felt, that night, a strange and sudden power stirring within me, an unusual daring I had not known before.
My hand moved slowly, slowly, upon the fastening of the lantern.
The old man, I imagine, must have stirred slightly upon his bed, for I heard him move at that very instant.
Perhaps he had heard some sound, for now he sat straight up in his bed.
I remained perfectly motionless where I stood, listening as intently as he listened for the source of that same disturbance.
I kept my position for a long, long hour without moving a single muscle.
In all this time I did not once hear him lie back down again upon his bed.
He was still sitting up, listening, as I myself had done, night after night, straining his ears against the deep, hollow silence of the darkened house.
Presently I heard a slight groan, and I knew it to be the groan of mortal terror.
I had felt that very same feeling myself, on many long, sleepless nights of my own.
I knew what the old man felt, though I chuckled quietly at heart.
I understood how his hair must have risen upon his aged and trembling head with a nameless, growing dread.
He had been trying, all this while, to convince himself that the sound was nothing.
Perhaps it was merely the wind in the chimney, he told himself, or a mouse crossing the floor behind the old, familiar walls.
He had been saying to himself, with these comforting explanations, that his own vague fears were groundless.
But he knew, I think, that Death himself now stood beside his bed in the darkness.
When I had waited a long time, very patiently, without hearing him lie back down, I resolved at last to open a small, small crack in the lantern.
So I opened it, cautiously, cautiously, until at length a single dim ray, like the thread of a spider, shot out and fell full upon the vulture eye.
It was open, wide, wide open, and I grew furious as I gazed upon it.
I saw it with perfect distinctness, all a dull, dreadful blue, with a hideous veil over it that chilled the very marrow in my bones.
I could see nothing else of the old man's face or body.
I had directed the ray, as if by instinct, precisely upon that one damned and accursed spot.

chapters.title: Chapter 3 — The Deed
paragraphs: And now, have I not already told you that what you mistake for madness is only over-acuteness of the senses?
For now, I say, there came to my ears a low, dull, quick sound, such as a watch makes when wrapped in cotton.
I knew that sound well, too, for it was the beating of the old man's heart.
It increased my fury, exactly as the beating of a drum stimulates the soldier into a reckless, blind courage.
But even now I restrained myself and kept perfectly still, scarcely breathing, holding the lantern motionless.
I tried as steadily as I could to keep the ray fixed precisely upon that dreadful eye.
Meanwhile the hellish beating of the heart increased, faster and faster, and louder and louder, every moment.
The old man's terror, I felt certain, must by now have been absolutely extreme.
It grew louder, I say, louder every moment — do you mark me well?
I have told you already that I am nervous, so very nervous, and dreadfully so.
Now, at that dead hour of the night, amid the fearful silence of that ancient house, so strange a noise as this excited me to an uncontrollable terror of my own.
Yet, for some minutes longer, I restrained myself and stood still, though the beating grew louder, louder still.
I thought the heart must surely burst, and then a new anxiety seized me, for I feared that some neighbor might hear the sound.
The old man's hour had come at last, and with a loud yell I threw open the lantern fully and leaped into the room.
He shrieked once, only once, before I could reach him.
In an instant I dragged him to the floor and pulled the heavy bed over him.
Then I smiled, gaily, for the deed itself was almost done, and the worst part of it, I dare say, was over at last.
But for many minutes still the heart beat on, with a muffled, faint sound.
This did not disturb me now, for it could not be heard through the wall by any neighbor passing outside.
At length it stopped, and the old man was dead.
I removed the bed and examined the corpse, and I placed my hand upon his heart, and held it there for many minutes.
I felt nothing whatsoever, not the smallest pulse of life remaining.
He was stone dead now, and his eye, I thought with a strange satisfaction, would trouble me no longer, ever again, for as long as I might live.
If you still think me mad, you will think so no longer once I describe the wise precautions I now took for the concealment and disposal of that lifeless body.
The night waned, and I worked in haste, but in silence.
First of all I dismembered the corpse, cutting off the head, the arms, and the legs, with careful, methodical strokes.
I then took up three planks from the flooring of the chamber and deposited all between the scantlings.
I replaced the boards so cleverly, so cunningly, that no human eye, not even his, could ever have detected anything wrong.
There was nothing at all to wash out, no stain of any kind, no blood-spot whatsoever.
I had been far too careful for that, and a tub had caught it all quite completely.
When I had made an end of these labors, it was four o'clock, still dark as midnight.
As the bell sounded the hour, there came a knocking at the street door below, loud and insistent.

chapters.title: Chapter 4 — The Confession
paragraphs: I went down to open it with a light heart, for what had I now to fear?
The man I had feared was safely hidden and would trouble no one, ever again, in this world.
Three men entered, introducing themselves, with perfect suavity, as officers of the police.
A shriek had been heard by a neighbor during the night, suspicion of foul play had been aroused, and information had accordingly been lodged at the police station.
I smiled, for what had I to fear, and I bade the gentlemen welcome.
I explained that the shriek had been my own, uttered in a dream, and that the old man, I added calmly, was absent in the country at present.
I led my visitors all over the house, and I bade them search, search well.
Eventually I led them to his very chamber, where I showed them his untouched treasures, secure and undisturbed in their proper places.
In the enthusiasm of my confidence I brought chairs into the very room, and desired them here to rest from their fatigues.
I myself, in the wild audacity of my perfect triumph, placed my own seat upon the very spot beneath which the corpse of the victim lay hidden.
The officers were satisfied, and my manner had convinced them entirely, and they sat and chatted of familiar things.
I answered cheerfully, at my perfect ease, though I felt myself growing pale and wished them gone at once.
My head ached, and I fancied a ringing in my ears, but still they sat, and still they chatted.
The ringing became more distinct, until at length I found that the noise was not within my own ears at all.
No doubt I now grew very pale, but I talked more fluently, and with a heightened voice.
Yet the sound increased, and what could I do, for it was a low, dull, quick sound, much such a sound as a watch makes when enveloped in cotton.
I gasped for breath, and yet the officers heard it not.
I talked more quickly, more vehemently, but the noise steadily increased, and I rose and argued about trifles, in a high key and with violent gesticulations.
Was it possible that they heard it not, for it grew louder, louder still?
Yet the men sat pleasantly, and smiled, and I thought them mocking my terror with their sly and unbearable derision.
Anything, I thought, was more tolerable than this cruel, unbearable agony.
I could bear those hypocritical smiles no longer, and I felt that I must scream or die that very moment.
And now, again, I heard the sound — louder, louder, louder!
“Villains!” I shrieked, “dissemble no more!
I admit the deed — tear up the planks!
Here, here — it is the beating of his hideous heart!”
